🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -0.95% (intraday, 7-year +14bp). At trading day 19 (last close) it was -1.10% against a five-campaign average of -1.19% at the same point — 1994-95, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.35%. The 10-year is +16bp since the hike vs a +16bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 4 of 4 signals: topping likely).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 719bp against a five-year average of 411bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +40bp and BB +35bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.31 → 0.52 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is untouched (+3bp).
  • Bank Earnings: 3 banks reported (BAC, MS, STT); no red flags. Credit broadly stable; deposit costs flat.
  • Stocks: Tech and small caps fell almost 2%; the Dow barely moved; Europe rose.
  • FX: The dollar index rose a little; the euro stays weak and the yen soft.
  • Technicals: The S&P is resting on its 50-day average; a close below it opens a deeper pullback.
  • Sectors: Money moved out of tech and into health care, staples and energy.
  • Credit/Spreads: High-grade debt is calm; the riskiest junk bonds are the most stressed since 2020.
  • Crisis: Overall stress is moderate, led by junk-credit decay and Iran-driven oil risk.
  • Inflation: Core inflation is near 2.5-3% but a quarter of prices rise above 5%.
  • Tech Bubble: Valuations are far from 2000 levels, but loose credit and calm markets resemble then.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Meta and Lam Research report next week; there is no confirmed big US IPO.
  • Iran: No October reports could be verified; the latest confirmed news is from mid-2026.
  • Warsh: Warsh's Fed dropped its easing bias; a rate hike stays possible, not certain.
  • Week Ahead: A heavy earnings week (Netflix, GE, Tesla, Meta) plus big Asian IPOs.
  • Outlook: Cautious near term; respect the S&P's 50-day average and the junk-bond stress.
  • Trades: Cut low-quality junk, favor defensives, and buy 10-year Treasuries.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 1 buy, 2 sell, 21 hold long, 21 stay out
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.64 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +91bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 95th pctile, +11bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Bottom line: Tech wobbles while junk-credit stress spreads; stay defensive until both calm down.

The PM session was a growth-led de-risking, not a broad panic. The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.880249% (-511.51) to 26692.87, the Russell 2000 fell 1.934275% to 2729.531 and the S&P 500 fell 1.108328% to 7718.94. The Dow fell only 0.09409697%. VIX rose 10.47806% to 16.87 from 15.27. Europe went the other way: STOXX 600 +0.4314893%, Euro Stoxx 50 +0.3787897% and FTSE 100 +0.6997905%. Leadership flipped sharply. Info Tech fell -2.62% and Comm Services -1.73%, while Health Care (+2.44%) and Staples (+2.38%) led. That is a classic defensive rotation. Treasuries rallied at the long end (10Y 5.1854%, -2.3bp; 30Y 5.5231%, -3.38bp) while the 2Y edged up to 4.7975%. The curve flattened to the computed 38.79bp 2s10s. The bigger story is in credit. The computed HY contagion panel puts the Caa-B gap at 719bp, the 100th percentile of its 5-year history against a 5y average of ~411bp. It has widened 202bp in 3 months, and the Caa index (1017bp) is the widest since 2020-04-24. The rot is now visibly climbing the quality ladder. Single-B OAS is +40bp over 1 month (298bp) and Ba is +35bp (189bp), so the stress has spread past CCC. It has NOT reached investment grade: IG OAS is 82bp, only +3bp in a month, still at the 8th percentile of history. The B-Ba gap (109bp) is still below its 5y average, so BB is moving with single-B rather than lagging it. The 63-day Caa/B correlation rose to 0.52 from 0.35 a month ago but is still below its 0.70 5y median. This is descriptive context, not a validated signal. Net sentiment: risk-off at the margin. Equity froth is coming out of tech, and the weakest borrowers are being repriced while top-tier credit stays complacent.

“When the junkiest bonds crack and the stretched tech names wobble on the same day, buy the boring stuff and wait.”

NY Harbor ULSD (US Diesel) — current: 492.74 cents/gal vs WTI

NY Harbor ULSD is at 492.74 cents/gal, at the 99.9th percentile with a z-score of 3.38. Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.64 vol points (17th percentile of the 42 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 99.1 (71th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 98bp (steeper by 22bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Cup test

COMPONENTLEVELDATE
Left rim6.79%2000-01-20
Cup base0.51%2020-08-04
Right rim5.30%2026-10-05

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (97bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 13 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 55/100 — The core trend is anchored but not falling to target, and the inflation is concentrated rather than broad. The median, trimmed-mean and sticky measures sit roughly between 2.2% and 2.8%. Most are flat-to-falling, and their history-relative ranking is shown separately as the computed Core-Trend Sub-Score. The breadth picture is less benign. The Dallas Fed distribution puts 13.2% of the PCE basket above 10% and 15.7% at 5-10%, so 28.9% of items are inflating above 5% (computed sum), versus 25.8% falling. Flexible CPI at 6.12% and rising, with oil near 95-106, keeps headline pressure alive. Core PCE at 3.00759% stays a full point above target. Persistence is moderate: an energy-driven upside tail on a sticky ~2.5-3% core.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (42x) ≈ 24% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The dot-com analogue fits the financing backdrop better than the price action. Credit and financial conditions are as loose as, or looser than, they were at the 2000 top, VIX is subdued, and margin debt is growing 33.7% YoY (46% of the 2000 surge). Equity froth itself is well short of that peak. The current cycle, anchored at Oct-2022, has run to about 243 on the computed index after 48 months. On the analog chart, the 1990-anchored dot-com path took 113 months to peak. Today's tech-led sell-off is happening while the junkiest credit is cracking (Caa-B at a record-wide 5y percentile). That combination of credit decay at the margin and loose headline conditions is late-cycle in character. The analyst-estimate inputs (top-10 concentration ~40%, CAPE ~39x, market cap/GDP ~215%, IPO froth 55, LT EPS growth 70) are unverified this run: no source was searched for them.

⚔️Iran War

I could not verify any October 2026 developments; searches returned nothing dated this month. The latest verifiable record: a two-week ceasefire was announced April 8, 2026, tied to reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Iran re-closed the strait in mid-April over the US blockade of its ports. US officials said in early May that the ceasefire was holding. In June, Iran again declared the strait closed while US officials said traffic continued. Separately, Just Security's July 22 edition reported 11 straight nights of US strikes and Iranian drone fire at US facilities in Kuwait, Jordan and Bahrain, so the ceasefire had broken down by then. The current status is unverified. Brent at 106.09 and WTI at 95.09 imply markets still price a meaningful supply-risk premium (inference).

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Hold with a hawkish bias, with a 25bp hike a live risk (analyst estimate; inference). This is based on the June record: he dropped the easing bias, refused to give forward guidance, and nine officials projected rates rising by end-2026. I could not verify the September decision.

~1 YEAR

Policy tighter than June's 3.50-3.75% range, likely via 1-2 hikes, plus a push for a smaller balance sheet and an overhaul of Fed communications (inference). This draws on his announced task forces on communications, balance sheet and the inflation framework.

Warsh's debut meeting on June 17, 2026 held at 3.50-3.75%. It removed forward guidance, and he said 'I can't give you any forward guidance about what we're going to do next.' The dot plot moved to 3.8% for end-2026 from 3.4%, implying a hike. He launched reviews of communications, balance sheet strategy, data use and the inflation framework. Inference: today's 2Y at 4.7975% sits well above that June range. Either markets price several more hikes, or tightening has already occurred since June; I could not verify which. Core PCE at 3.00759% gives him no cover to ease. Expect data-dependent, guidance-light meetings where surprises are more likely than under prior chairs.
